3.0.s.en: 1. To every thing there is a season:

3.0.0.en: 1 To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: 2 A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; 3 A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; 4 A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; 5 A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather stones; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; 6 A time to get, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; 7 A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; 8 A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace. 9 What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboureth? 10 I have seen the travail which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised in it.

3.0.1.en: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" [1].

3.0.2.en: Our life, with all its circumstances and conditions, proceeds according to an ordered schedule that fulfils God's purposes at the right time. We must perform our duties faithfully and prepare for the future, that we may see God's plan for us. By a divine plan God created the world for our sake, and at the right time He sent the fathers and the prophets and gave us the Law, and at the appointed time salvation was accomplished by the Cross, and by heavenly wisdom God cares for every small and great thing in your life, so that even the number of the hairs of your head does not escape His care.

3.0.3.en: In other words, the history of the whole world, and the history of your own life in particular, with all its details, are links in a chain of events that God arranges... You must live in a spirit of faithfulness, working with all your energies and living with joy and gladness, trusting in God who orders your life; for by yourself you cannot do anything, whatever your desire and whatever your abilities... for "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" [1].

3.0.4.en: a. Origen explains how the Law has its time and the covenant of grace has its time, saying:

3.0.5.en: ["To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." There is a time for gathering good pearls, and another time, after gathering them, for discovering the pearl of great price, when it befits a man to go and sell all that he has to buy that pearl. For just as a man who wants to become wise in the words of truth must first learn the principles, and then pass beyond the elementary teaching, which he esteems with all esteem yet does not remain fixed at that point, but honors it at the outset and then seeks perfection. He acknowledges gratitude for what he was first taught, because it benefited him greatly! So he who understands the Law and the Prophets with full mastery knows that they are elementary teaching for grasping the Gospel in its fullness and grasping the meaning of all the words and works of Christ.

3.0.6.en: Origen b. St. Gregory of Nazianzus was attacked because he asked that speaking about God with others be done wisely, in a suitable manner and at the right time. He defended himself, saying: [I do not forbid the constant remembrance of God, but only speaking about God, not because there is anything wrong in it in itself, but when it is presented in an unreasonable manner; and I do not forbid all teaching but ask for moderation in it. It is like honey: if a man eats it greedily in excess, it causes vomiting, though it is honey. Solomon says: "To every thing there is a season," and in my belief what is good no longer remains good if it is used in a way that is not good. It is like one who plucks a flower out of the winter season, and as a man's garment does not suit a woman, and the opposite is also true. Athletic games do not befit a place of mourning, nor tears a place of merriment; we all do not accept a thing out of its time, while we honor it if it is used at the right time. Is it not so, my friends and brethren?].

3.0.7.en: c. St. Gregory defended Pope Athanasius the Apostolic, who hid himself in the time of distress, when the Arians tried to kill him, and appeared at the right time, saying: [I approve of Solomon's wise counsel that to every thing there is a season. Therefore he hid himself for a time, fleeing in the time of war, to appear in the time of peace which soon came afterward]. He also defended his own flight when he was accused of defeat, saying: [To every thing there is a season: there is a time for defeat (for flight), and, as I think, a season to every purpose. It is better to be defeated with honor than to win and prevail by a dangerous, unlawful victory].

3.0.8.en: Wise Solomon presents several examples to confirm that to every thing there is a season:

3.1.0.en: a. "A time to be born, and a time to die" [2]: God in His love for us has fixed the time of our birth and also the time of our departure from this world; this does not mean that we should not care for our bodily life on the pretext that God has appointed the hour of our departure and that our care will be of no avail. The Lord Christ asked His disciples to flee when they were persecuted, not out of fear of death, but for their own safety. The Arians attacked Pope Athanasius because he fled from them when they tried to kill him. In his defense he said: [Father Isaac said to his son Esau, "Behold now, I am old, I know not the day of my death" (Gen 27:2). But our Lord, being God the Word of the Father, knew the time that He Himself appoints for all, and knew the time of His sufferings, which He Himself determined for His body; yet because He became man for our sake, He hid Himself when they sought (to kill Him) before the appointed time came, as we do. And when He was persecuted He fled, avoiding the plots of His enemies, and passed through the midst of them].

3.1.1.en: If the Lord has fixed the time of our birth and the time of our death, yet He puts on our shoulders the responsibility of caring for our temporal life and the health and safety of our body; He also fixes the time of the death of our old man and the birth of our new man, where the two take place together at one time in Baptism (Rev 6:4-6), and we too are bound to work by the Spirit of God, striving not to live according to the works of the old man but according to the new man.

3.1.2.en: * In the very same moment you died and were born; and this water of salvation became at once your grave and your mother, and what Solomon said about others has become fitting for you also, for he says, "A time to conceive and a time to die." But for you it happens otherwise, for there is a time to die followed by a time to be born, and the two happen together, since your (spiritual) birth goes side by side with your death.

3.1.3.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem Since there is a time for birth, let us prepare to depart, for we do not know the time that God appoints for us; so we live in a world with no stability, not securing our life even for one coming moment.

3.1.4.en: * You were born, and therefore you die: if you flee from death, or avoid it, or push it away from you, you cannot postpone it or keep it from you. It is bound to come, even if you refuse; and at an hour you do not know...

3.1.5.en: Since here you cannot wish not to die, choose to be with the living, lest you die forever...

3.1.6.en: You who do all you can to postpone death a little, do something so that you may not die forever...

3.1.7.en: St. Augustine b. "A time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted" [2]: there is a set time for planting trees and a special time for uprooting them; so also God plants certain nations and allows them authority and power, and also allows them to be uprooted. Nations have arisen of which no one could have thought that they would decline, but in moments God allowed them to collapse, so that man may realize the vanity of the whole world.

3.1.8.en: The believer realizes that there is a time for planting holy thoughts and a time for uprooting evil and unseemly thoughts, where he learns a life of constant prayer, supplication and perseverance, and reliance on the free grace of God, awaiting the sanctification and purification of his thoughts by the Holy Spirit of God.

3.1.9.en: Let us be planted like an olive tree in the house of the Lord, and let us be uprooted from the field of this passing world!

3.2.0.en: c. "A time to kill, and a time to heal" [3]: perhaps he meant by this the killing of the old man and the healing of the new man, which is accomplished in the waters of Baptism (Rom 6:4-6).

3.2.1.en: Perhaps he means that need sometimes requires great firmness in judgment, where a sentence of death is sometimes passed for the edification of the community and to rescue it from those who pose a grave danger to it, and the matter may call for pardon and gentleness.

3.2.2.en: It is noted here that he begins with killing and follows it with healing, to show that firmness does not carry a spirit of vengeance and anger, but is for edification and healing.

3.2.3.en: Let us not fear the vanity of the world, for although we see it as a killing of our temporal life, it carries healing for our eternal life. Let us die that we may live in the Lord forever!

3.2.4.en: d. "A time to break down, and a time to build up" [3]: we must not stop at the negative side: the breaking down of the old man with his works and thoughts, but must extend to the positive side, which is the building up of the inner new man and his virtues. It is not enough, for example, to break down hatred; love must be established.

3.2.5.en: He begins with breaking down because we cannot set up a lofty building unless we dig the foundations, and as St. Augustine says, by humility we break down the pride of our haughtiness and lay the foundations of the building of the Spirit that rises to the heavens!

3.2.6.en: He also says: [The medicine for your sickness is the humility of Christ... Do not exalt yourself but humble yourself if you wish to be healed. And if you wish to reach the height of God, seek Him first in His humility... when you take His humility and rise with Him... Look at the tree, how its growth begins from below and then rises into the air. Its roots are in the earth and its branches toward heaven. Can the tree rise into the air if it does not rely on its roots in the earth? If you wish to reach the heavens apart from humility and love, you have no root. Then you seek destruction, not growth...].

3.2.7.en: The time for breaking down has come, for the Creator of the whole world declares: heaven and earth shall pass away (Mt 5:8), and the time for building comes, where there is a new heaven and a new earth (Rev 21:1) and a new city (Rev 21:2).

3.3.0.en: e. "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance" [4]: as we practice weeping over our souls by being crucified with our Lord Jesus Christ, and mourning over our sins, we enjoy the joy of the Resurrection and the gladness (laughter) of the heavenly beings, and the dances of the soul, rejoicing in the work of Christ risen from the dead in us. The psalmist says: "Weeping may endure for a night, but joy (singing) cometh in the morning" (Ps 30:5).

3.3.1.en: There is a time to weep, for as long as we are in this world, the valley of tears, it befits us to offer constant repentance for our sins and daily weaknesses, so that when the day of the Lord comes there will be no sorrow nor crying nor pain (Rev 21:4).

3.3.2.en: * If you weep here you receive rest with every consolation, and there, if you weep, you go to torment...

3.3.3.en: * Weep here a little, lest you weep there forever in the outer darkness...

3.3.4.en: * Weep when you pray, that you may find rest...

3.3.5.en: * By tears, Hannah received Samuel the prophet from God...

3.3.6.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian * Blessed are those who weep for the sake of truth, for through their tears they continually see the face of God.

3.3.7.en: * He who sees himself dead in sins does not need to learn how to weep.

3.3.8.en: * There are tears that burn and inflame, and others that gladden and make flourish...

3.4.0.en: St. Isaac the Syrian f. "A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather stones" [5]: the scattering of stones or rolling them on the earth (according to the Septuagint) points to the acceptance of the pagan Gentiles, and as St. Jerome says: [God raised up from the hard stones of the Gentiles children to Abraham, so they became holy stones rolling on the earth (Zech 9:16 LXX)]. If the time has come for the pagan Gentiles to accept the faith and bear witness to the Lord Christ on earth... there will come the time when all the living stones are gathered to reveal the heavenly temple of God, of which it is said: "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; in whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord" (Eph 2:20-21). "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God" (Rev 3:12). By faith the spiritual building of the temple of the Lord began with living stones, "to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ" (1 Pet 2:5), and the completion of the building is accomplished by its revelation on the day of the Lord as a heavenly building that remains forever. In other words, let the world be broken down; in its breaking down our inner building is not broken down, but is revealed in greatest power at the coming of the Lord on the clouds and our entrance into His heavenly glory.

3.4.1.en: The scattering and gathering of stones point to the demolition of an old building and its replacement by a new one... So if the world with its vanity collapses, we are not troubled, for we enjoy a new world, the abiding city which has the foundations, whose maker and builder is God (Heb 11:1).

3.4.2.en: The scattering of stones also points to filling up fields by casting stones into them and burying them (2 Kgs 3:19, 25), and the gathering of them points to reclaiming the fields and making them fit for sowing.

3.4.3.en: Perhaps it means here the demolition of the building of the Old Testament to be replaced by the Church of the New Testament, and the demolition of the field of the old people so that the field of the New Testament may arise, extending to the ends of the world... But the Church will not remain confined to this temporal world; rather she awaits the collapse of the material world and the passing away of what is visible, that we may enjoy what is heavenly and enjoy the invisible God... then we shall see Him face to face.

3.4.4.en: Stones are also gathered to make a memorial monument as a sign of establishing a covenant between two parties, or as a memorial of great events, like the pillar which Jacob set up (Gen 28:18; 31:52), and the heaps of stones over Achan and Absalom, or for erecting triumphal arches as a sign of victory; and the scattering of stones points to the breaking of the covenant or the removal of memorial triumphal arches.

3.4.5.en: If by sin the stones of our covenant with God are scattered and the triumphal arches against the enemy of good are torn down, let us hasten and gather the stones by the Spirit of God and renew the covenant in the merits of the Blood, and quickly set up the triumphal arches, for the time is shortened and the days are evil, and the world is ending and passing away.

3.4.6.en: g. "A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing" [5]. In the previous examples he mostly begins with the painful matter followed by the joyful: he begins with birth followed by death (since the day of departure is sweeter than the day of birth), he begins with killing followed by healing; breaking down followed by building up, weeping followed by laughing, mourning followed by dancing, scattering stones followed by gathering them; so why does he begin here with embracing followed by separation? Is separation better and sweeter? Some Fathers see here a reference to the loftiness of the virgin life; the Old Testament sanctified marriage and urged it as an embrace of love... and everyone awaited the coming of the Messiah, born of woman, hoping he might come from his offspring according to the flesh; then the New Testament came, which, though it sanctified marriage, urges virginity all the more, as a separation from embracing so that the believer may devote all his energies to worship and to witnessing for the joyful Kingdom of God. It is a call not for everyone, but "he that is able to receive it, let him receive it." The Apostle Paul says: "For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that... But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord: but he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife" (1 Cor 7:7, 32).

3.4.7.en: * How shall I explain the great merit and high dignity which the believers and holy virginity have in the sight of God; for the time has come to refrain from embracing. When there is a great multitude from all the nations filling the number of the saints, is there any need to practice the earthly pleasure of the body in order to give offspring?!

3.4.8.en: * In former times there was a time to embrace, and finally it is a time to refrain from embracing.

3.4.9.en: * As for the Christians of our age, who have been freed from the bond of marriage, since they have the power to abstain from any bodily relations, they see that the time has come of which it is written, "A time to refrain from embracing," and that it is not the time of embracing; would they not rather choose to preserve their virginity or widowhood?!

3.4.10.en: St. Augustine This is the symbolic understanding; as for the literal interpretation, it means that those who embrace, that is, the married, will inevitably have their married life dissolved in this world by the death of one of the parties, so that he who married becomes as one who has not married... This is the nature of the vain world, as the Apostle says that those who use it are as though they did not use it, and those who marry as though they did not marry.

3.5.0.en: h. "A time to get (to seek), and a time to lose" [6]: if a man receives temporal blessings, he gives thanks, and if he loses them, he blesses God who gave and took away, saying with righteous Job: "The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord" (Job 1:21).

3.5.1.en: Perhaps getting points to the Old Testament, with its promises of many temporal blessings (Deut 28), and losing to the New Testament, where believers rejoice in the Cross and are glad to give up willingly what they have, counting everything as refuse that they may win Christ (Phil 3:8).

3.5.2.en: If our coming into the world is a gain as a divine gift, our departure from it is a loss, that we may gain what is greater: the new heaven and the new earth (Rev 21:1)!

3.5.3.en: i. "A time to keep, and a time to cast away" [6]: there is a time when a thing is kept and man tries to preserve it, but when he feels that repairing it costs him much, he throws it away and gets rid of it to acquire something newer. So we acquire our temporal life and keep it by the Holy Spirit of God, who renews and sanctifies it, but at the right time our temporal life is cast away that we may acquire a higher and more lasting life!

3.5.4.en: So also man lived in former times under the shadows of the Law and its symbols, keeping it literally like one who preserves pearls; but now that the Lord Christ, the pearl of great price, has come, he casts away the literalism of the Law and leaves the shadows, to live in the fullness of truth, acquiring the new life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

3.6.0.en: j. "A time to rend, and a time to sew" [7]: perhaps rending points to intensity of grief, for the ancients were accustomed to rend their garments when severe calamities occurred, as Reuben did when he returned and did not find Joseph in the pit (Gen 37:29), and as Job did when his trial grew severe (Job 1:20). And sewing points to joy and the return of peace, for at times of joy all the members of the family take care to sew new clothes fitting for the joy.

3.6.1.en: Rending also points to our separation from evil habits, and sewing to our attachment to the virtuous, holy life in the Lord. St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [I believe the meaning of the saying "A time to rend, and a time to sew" is that we must separate completely from everything to which we were bound in our evils, and cleave to what is good].

3.6.2.en: Perhaps rending points to our withdrawal from the wicked who cause stumbling, and sewing to the fellowship of the heavenly beings and the saints in Christ Jesus, the Head of all.

3.6.3.en: k. "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak" [7]: he begins with silence, for it is not fitting to utter a word except after silence and serious thought.

3.6.4.en: Silence points to the hidden life of contemplation, and speaking points to witnessing to the Savior before others and serving them, for holy silence is not enough; we must also speak the edifying word of the Lord.

3.6.5.en: * The Preacher mentions first the time that is needed for silence, and then allows a time for speech.

3.6.6.en: When, then, and in what matters is silence better?

3.6.7.en: Those who are concerned with conduct say that silence is always better than speech. And Paul distinguishes the times needed for speech and those needed for silence. Sometimes he recommends silence and at other times speech.

3.6.8.en: When the time for speech comes he says: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth" (Eph 4:29).

3.6.9.en: And he recommends silence, saying: "Let your women keep silence in the churches... And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home" (1 Cor 14:34-35).

3.6.10.en: He reveals to us the suitable time for speech, saying: "Lie not one to another" (Col 3:9, etc.), "speak every man truth with his neighbour" (Eph 4:25).

3.6.11.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * When the mind approaches matters that surpass it, it is a time for deep silence, for it must rather preserve its admiration or amazement at that power which is not grasped or searched out in the depths of our consciences. And realizing that these great men speak not of God's (nature) but of His works, he says: "Who can speak of the mighty acts of the Lord?", "I will shew forth all thy marvellous works," "One generation shall praise thy works to another" (Ps 106:2; 9:1; 145:4)... Thus speaking is of God's (works); but as for approaching His essence, it is a time for silence.

3.6.12.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa We must be silent in order to contemplate God and enjoy His shining upon us; then we go forth with words of grace, and bear witness to His work in our life and His rich grace and the opening of the door of His Kingdom to every human being. It also befits us not to speak much about divine matters that surpass the mind and cannot be expressed.

3.6.13.en: The Fathers, through the Gospel mind, advise us to keep stillness and flee from much vain talk, which robs the soul of its calm and its fellowship with God.

3.6.14.en: As the Fathers warn us of vain talk that spoils the peace of the soul, so they warn us also of vain silence, which is not accompanied by prayer and fellowship with God and vigilance for the sake of the Kingdom.

3.6.15.en: St. John Chrysostom says that there is good speech and idle speech, as there is good silence and idle silence... We must know when to be silent and when to speak, and how to be silent and about what to speak.

3.6.16.en: * The more a man flees from chattering with his tongue, the more his mind is enlightened, so that he can sort out and evaluate deep thoughts, because the mind is confused by chatter.

3.6.17.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * If we are to give account for every idle word, let us be careful not to utter it; and let us also beware of idle silence!

3.6.18.en: But there is an effective silence, like the silence of Susanna, who by her silence did more than if she had spoken. For by her silence before men, she spoke with God, and she found no stronger proof of her chastity than silence. Her conscience spoke when she found no word to utter, and she did not ask for judgment from men, for she had the Lord's testimony. Therefore she longed that God Himself would acquit her, knowing that He cannot be deceived by any means.

3.6.19.en: The Lord Himself also worked in silence to accomplish the salvation of mankind.

3.6.20.en: David asked that his soul not be occupied with rigid silence but with watchfulness and attentiveness.

3.6.21.en: St. Ambrose * Nevertheless there is a time to speak of those things by which we advance in virtue in our life.

3.7.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa l. "A time to love, and a time to hate" [8]: in the meekness of love St. Demiana was submissive to her father Mark, governor of Bruls, and when he denied the faith, with a firmness resembling hatred she told him that if he did not return to the faith by repentance she would not count him her father, nor would she be his daughter.

3.7.1.en: Let us love everyone in the Lord, and let us be firm so as to seem as if hating, for the sake of our salvation and theirs.

3.7.2.en: m. "A time of war, and a time of peace" [8]; the matter sometimes needs a firmness that resembles war; then we must know how to reconcile and bind up wounds. Therefore he mentioned peace after war, so that we do not stop at firmness and severity as long as we can. Even if the Church disciplines heretics, she awaits with longing their return to the truth and their reconciliation.

3.7.3.en: Perhaps the most wonderful example of this is St. Cyril the Great, whom some scholars unfortunately attack as a violent leader against Nestorius; we read in one of his letters to Nestorius that there is no one who loves him as he does.

3.8.0.en: 11 He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set eternity in their heart, without which man cannot find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end. 12 I know that there is no good in them, but for a man to rejoice, and to do good in his life. 13 And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God. 14 I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth it, that men should fear before him. 15 That which hath been is of old; and that which is to be hath of old been; and God requireth that which is past.

3.8.1.en: It is clear from the previous examples that:

3.8.2.en: a. To every thing there is a season... as though nothing is good in itself, but according to our use of it in the fitting measure and at the fitting time.

3.8.3.en: * The things we use in certain circumstances and at suitable times, so that they sanctify us... are things that are neither good nor evil, such as marriage, farming, wealth, withdrawal into the desert, vigils, reading Holy Scripture and meditating on it, and fasting... For these things, or some of them, our forefathers commanded us to carry out with discernment, and to pay attention to the motive for them, the place of carrying them out, the means and the time. For when we carry them out in a suitable manner they become good and fitting, and if we use them with deviation they become evil and harmful... Fasting is reckoned evil for those who expect by it the praise of men...

3.8.4.en: Abba Theonas b. To every thing there is a season... so nothing remains eternal!

3.8.5.en: c. Since to every thing there is a season, man is unable to grasp God's purposes and His surpassing arrangements and to change them.

3.8.6.en: d. The previous examples point to God's work with us, for the new time has come in which we have passed from the age of the Law to the age of grace, from the stage of spiritual childhood to maturity, from shadow and letter to truth and spirit, from the time of temporal gains to the joyful loss for the sake of Him who gave His life for us, from the season of strife and enmity with God to reconciliation with Him as members of His household! e. God, who created time and is not subject to it, for the sake of the arrangement of our salvation submitted by His will to time, when He took our nature and accepted death in His body for us.

3.8.7.en: f. If God, as a Creator who loves mankind, "hath made every thing beautiful in his time" [11], and all that He created is good and well ordered, yet He lifts us above time... He submitted to time in order to lift us above time, for "he hath set eternity in their heart, without which man cannot find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end" [11].

3.8.8.en: The word "eternity" here is one of the words around which most dispute has arisen in the Book of Ecclesiastes. Some have suggested that it is "the universe," others "mystery" or "forgetfulness," and others have reckoned it derived from the Ugaritie root "glm," meaning "becomes dark," saying that God made everything beautiful and fitting but man is unable to grasp the mysteries of God's plan and wisdom because darkness has settled upon his mind and heart.

3.9.0.en: g. Lest anyone think that the lifting of the heart to heaven or to eternity pushes us into gloom or into contempt for temporal life, he returns to affirm that all we receive or practice with wisdom is a divine gift: "I know that there is no good in them, but for a man to rejoice, and to do good in his life. And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God" [12-13].

3.9.1.en: The Preacher cannot be accused of any materialistic or hedonistic tendencies, that is, that pleasure or enjoyment is the only good in this worldly life; rather, as we said before, he carries a tendency of praise through which the believer feels that all he has in his hands is a gift of God, even eating and drinking, so he finds enjoyment in life because it bears the imprints of God's surpassing love. He feels that the circumstances he lives in and the resources in his hands are the best that suit him in this life as a preparation for eternal life, so he lives his life in a spirit of praise and joy.

3.10.0.en: h. "To every thing there is a season": God dealt with the men of the Old Testament as children in faith, urging them to holiness with temporal blessings, while with the men of the New Testament He urges them as men to holiness by bearing the Cross and sharing His sufferings; yet in His dealings, His covenants and His love He has not changed. We change and alter our position toward Him, therefore it is said: "I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it" [14].

3.11.0.en: And lest it be thought that God's dealings with the Church of the New Testament are at the expense of the men of the Old Testament, he says: "God requireth that which is past" [15].

3.12.0.en: 16 And moreover I saw under the sun that in the place of truth there is injustice, and in the place of justice there is oppression! 17 I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work. 18 I said in mine heart concerning the estate of the sons of men, that God tests them, to show them that they themselves are like a beast. 19 For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for both are vanity. 20 All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again. 21 Who knoweth the spirit of the sons of men, whether it goeth upward? and the spirit of the beast, whether it goeth downward to the earth? 22 Wherefore I perceived that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?

3.12.1.en: If to every thing there is a season [1], and if the good God made every thing beautiful in its time [11], then the corruption that has come upon the world is not from the nature of the world itself, but through man's injustice and oppression of his fellow man.

3.12.2.en: What witness to the vanity of the world is like injustice occupying the place of truth, and oppression the place of justice [16]? Corruption spreads into the depths of the courts of justice! But the Preacher believes in God's just judgment. The corruption of the world does not mean that things proceed in an arbitrary way without restraint; rather God awaits the right time to judge the righteous and the wicked [17]. "For there is a time there for every purpose and for every work" [17]. In other words, if man by his corruption has wronged the world, in that he did not put everything in its proper time and place, so that injustice occupied the place of justice... yet God intervenes to set the situation right, but also in His own time.

3.12.3.en: The natural man thinks that man and beast are subject to death with no distinction between them; so does the spirit of man go upward and the spirit of the beast go downward under the earth?

3.12.4.en: Even if death comes upon the righteous and the wicked, upon man and animal, yet the righteous man, having cleaved to his Creator, does not fear death, which is the last door that separates him from his God.
